prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large ensembles, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B041 with Katori and Ye as a single part, and round 1 has made me more, not less, confident in the structure of the case. What the lattice clock offers is a measurement capability that did not exist before: the magic-wavelength condition lets one hold a very large number of neutral atoms tightly enough to suppress Doppler and recoil effects without perturbing the clock transition, and that combination is what gives both the systematic uncertainty and the statistical stability at the 1e-18 level. This is not a single group's claim. Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks in several countries are compared routinely and agree, and that independent reproduction is the evidence standard I trust most. In answer to the chair's first question, what it has already taught us: frequency comparisons resolving gravitational redshift over millimetre-scale height differences, increasingly stringent bounds on drifts of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark-matter couplings, and clock networks used for relativistic geodesy. I should be honest that these are bounds and demonstrations, not a deviation from known physics, and I would not let the citation claim more. The citation should be built around the lattice clock itself, as Olsson, Pearce and Lindroth ask, and should not speak of precision clocks in general. That wording is also the best answer to the overlap objection. The 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb as the tool that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped ions and photons. The lattice clock is a third thing, namely many-atom interrogation with an engineered cancellation of the trap shift, and it has been the route to the best fractional uncertainties and stability. Two names suit the lineage: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye for demonstrating that the platform scales to the present level of accuracy and stability with many-body and collisional effects brought under control.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain and I have not talked myself out of them. First, overlap and framing: Danielsson, Mehlig and Johansson ranked B041 seventh, and Danielsson says no deviation from known physics has yet been seen, so a committee that wants a discovery about nature will find the case closer to a superb instrument. Second, credit is not perfectly clean. PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, Takamoto, and the ytterbium and mercury communities all contributed decisively to the accuracy race, and two names cannot reflect that. Third, Ye's frequency-comb work was part of the 2005 prize background, and the overlap could be raised against him specifically. Fourth, the redefinition of the second has not been decided. I do not think that should be a maturity condition, because the physics and the inter-laboratory agreement already exist and the metrological decision is a separate institutional process, but I recognise reasonable members could weigh it differently. Finally, the early-demonstration dates and the first 1e-18 evaluations are quoted from memory by all of us and must be verified before a citation is finalised.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B032 with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, values predictions confirmed by nature, and in the chair's discussion says no deviation from known physics has yet been seen with lattice clocks, while ranking B041 seventh.
responses.response: I take your objection as a scientific one and not a mere overlap worry, and I think it deserves a direct answer. A clock does not need to find a deviation in order to have changed what can be observed: the millimetre-scale redshift measurement, bounds on constants and dark-matter couplings at levels that could not be reached before, and the agreement of independent species at 1e-18 are results about nature, even if they are null results so far. Two limits on my side. I would not word the citation as discovery of new physics, and I accept that your criterion, a confirmed prediction, fits B032 more tightly. But the magic-wavelength condition is also a prediction confirmed by experiment, and the uncertainty budgets are its test. On B032 itself, I would not oppose Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan if the 3D ARPES priority were established, but I cannot judge that chronology, and I do not want to see a trio chosen to cover 2D and 3D when the record on Hasan against other ARPES groups is unchecked. A citation anchored on the 2D quantum spin Hall state with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp seems to me the safer cut, if B032 were the outcome.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B032 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the one candidate where model, prediction and decisive experiment line up, but accepts that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu credit gaps leave the chain incomplete, and he lists the pending redefinition of the second as a maturity question for B041.
responses.response: I agree that B032 has the cleaner conceptual story, and your trio is the better B032 cut in my view because it follows the founding Z2 papers and the first experimental realisation. Where we differ is on what to do with an incomplete credit chain. For B041 the two names cover the idea and the demonstration that it scales, and the gaps are about who ran the race, whereas for B032 you concede that the HgTe proposal that guided the experiment is outside every proposed trio. That is a gap in the causal chain itself. On the redefinition, I raised it myself in round 1, and having thought about it again I do not think it should delay recognition. The optical clocks already meet the performance requirements and have been compared across continents, and what remains is a metrological and institutional decision. If you would accept that argument, your seventh-place ranking of B041 would be a question of preference between a concept and an instrument, which I respect, and no longer a question of maturity.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B031 for Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf, discloses that he is the member closest to circuit QED, and names B041 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Thank you for the disclosure. The chair asks whether I would accept B031 if timing were not an issue, and my answer is that I ranked it third because the physics of strong coupling and dispersive readout is real and has been reproduced in many laboratories, which is the standard I apply. My reservations are two. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits has just recognised the neighbouring foundation, and I think the committee will find it hard to explain a second circuit prize so soon as a distinct discovery rather than the architecture that built on it. Credit is also hard to cut, because Girvin and Huang co-authored the 2004 proposal and the Yale and ETH groups shared the experimental work, so the Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf cut is the field's convention, not a settled attribution. I would keep B031 as my second alternative. On recusal, I would not insist on it; a disclosure that the committee records, and a discount of your ranking, seem proportionate to me, since you named no personal tie to the candidates. I add that my own WACQT role overlaps institutionally with yours, and I disclose that below.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B041, asks that the citation say what is learned about nature, and leaves open a third lattice-clock name.
responses.response: I accept your request on the citation, within the limit of what is true: it should say lattice clock, magic wavelength and the 1e-18 level, and the accompanying material should list the relativistic, constants and dark-matter tests as what the instrument has already delivered. On the third name, I would hold at two. Takamoto, Lemonde, Le Targat and the PTB and NIST groups all made real contributions, but a third lattice-clock name would have to be defended against the others, and I cannot construct a principled line between them. I would rather say plainly in the public explanation that the accuracy race had many participants than invent a third laureate. I would ask you, as a theorist who has computed these level shifts, to check my claim that the many-body and collisional shifts in the lattice were the decisive step toward 1e-18 and that it was brought under control mainly by the JILA programme.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B032 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, values the agreement between measured spectra and first-principles theory, and says that B041 and B046 are cleaner on attribution if the B032 chain proves too contested.
responses.response: I value the point about measured spectra agreeing with first-principles calculations, because it is the same kind of evidence I trust in the clock case, where the uncertainty budgets rest on atomic-structure calculations of the blackbody and lattice shifts that experiments then check. On the chair's third question, my answer is that I would treat clean attribution as the weightier criterion only when the scientific cases are comparable, and I do not think that applies here: B032 has a stronger conceptual claim than B041 and I have said so. What decides it for me is that B041's credit problem is about breadth, while B032's is about a missing step. You say that B041 would be your second alternative, and I would be content with B032 as the fallback for the committee if members who prefer it can settle the Mele or Hasan question explicitly, as the chair asks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges optical lattice clocks to be sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or whether the three members who ranked it seventh hold an objection I have not answered.

The first realisation of the strontium lattice clock and the first 1e-18 evaluations are quoted from memory by me and by others, and I have not checked the dates or the credit against the record, so the order of Katori and Ye's contributions relative to other groups must be verified.
Whether two names suffice for B041 given the contributions of PTB, SYRTE, NIST and the Japanese groups, and whether Ye's comb background is a real overlap.
Whether the still-pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a maturity condition, on which I think not, but on which members can reasonably differ.
For B032 I cannot judge the priority chronology between Kane-Mele and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang or Hasan's 3D ARPES priority, which limits how firmly I can support it as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B041: I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye. My PhD advisor Sune Svanberg and a stay in John Hall's laboratory connect me to the broader laser-spectroscopy community from which this field grew, and I disclose that. For B031, my WACQT leadership role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers and Goran Johansson, and my rare-earth quantum-memory work is adjacent to superconducting-circuit quantum information; I flag this because B031 is my second alternative. I have no tie to the B032 candidates.
